sites.name: Saints John Mine & Mill
overview: A historic mine-and-mill complex near Montezuma with extensive collapsed timber, masonry, waste-rock, and industrial remains. The surviving landscape helps distinguish the mine workings from the mill and other industrial components.

timeline.text: Saints John developed as an important silver-lead-zinc mining complex in the Montezuma district.
Surviving ruins and field documentation help interpret the relationship between the mine workings, mill, and industrial remains.

features.name: Mill / Industrial Ruins
features.note: The surviving collapsed timber and masonry are consistent with the documented Saints John industrial complex; individual building functions are still being resolved.

features.name: Mine Workings
features.note: The broader Saints John property includes mine workings on the surrounding mountain in addition to the mill and industrial remains.

sites.name: Wellington Mine
overview: The Wellington was one of the major hard-rock mining operations in French Gulch east of Breckenridge. Historically separate from the neighboring Oro Mine, the two properties were combined in 1907 as the Wellington-Oro complex.
The operation is especially useful for understanding changes in mining and milling technology, with extensive underground workings and several generations of ore-processing equipment.

timeline.text: Major lode-mining activity developed in French Gulch, including the Wellington and Oro properties.
The previously separate Wellington and Oro mines were combined into the Wellington-Oro operation.
A gravity mill was built to concentrate ore.
A roasting and magnetic-separation plant was constructed for zinc-ore treatment.
Flotation technology replaced the older roasting and magnetic-separation process.
The earlier gravity mill ceased operation.
Mining activity continued intermittently after the main historic production period.
Treatment facilities address contaminated water draining from historic workings.

moreHistory: EPA historical studies describe the Wellington-Oro as the largest lode-mining operation in French Gulch, with more than 12 miles of underground workings.
The successive milling systems illustrate how operators adapted to changing ore types and metallurgical technology.
The Wellington and Oro began as separate mines. Their later combination is historically important, but the original identities should not be erased.
Modern remediation is part of the site’s continuing history and has altered portions of the industrial landscape.

sites.name: Pennsylvania Mine
overview: The Pennsylvania Mine is a historic hard-rock mine complex on the south side of Peru Creek near Montezuma. U.S. Geological Survey reporting identifies it as one of the most productive mines in the Montezuma quadrangle.

The vein was discovered in 1879, production peaked around 1893, and the property continued operating through difficult periods that closed many neighboring mines. The site is also important to modern water-quality work because mine drainage contributes acidic, metal-rich water to Peru Creek.

timeline.text: The Pennsylvania vein was discovered south of Decatur in the Peru Creek mining area.
The mine reached the height of its historic production and continued operating through the lean years that followed the silver panic.
The consolidated Pennsylvania property continued intermittent production of gold, silver, lead, copper, and zinc ores.
USGS studies of Peru Creek document acidic, metal-rich drainage from the Pennsylvania Mine and evaluate its contribution to downstream metal loading.

moreHistory: Historic USGS reporting records the Pennsylvania as one of the most productive properties in the Montezuma quadrangle.
Multiple mine levels, portals, waste dumps, timber remains, and the lower processing area preserve the layout of a substantial mountain mining complex.

features.name: Upper Workings
features.note: USGS photography documents upper workings of the Pennsylvania Mine in the headwaters of Peru Creek.

features.name: Mine Portals / Adits
features.note: Multiple openings and mine levels are associated with the Pennsylvania property.

features.name: Lower Processing Area
features.note: The lower industrial area is historically connected to the Pennsylvania property and remains distinct from the higher mine workings.

sites.name: Quail Mine
overview: The Quail Mine is a documented high-altitude hard-rock mine on the west slope of Collier Mountain, about a mile east of Montezuma. USGS reporting places the workings near 12,000 feet and describes two principal adits connected by a raise.

The Quail vein was discovered in the 1890s. Historic records document lead-silver ore shipments in the 1910s, and a Colorado mining report still listed the property as a lead-silver operation in 1952.

timeline.text: Philip Bianchi is reported to have discovered the Quail vein, and lead ore was shipped from the upper tunnel.
Historic reporting records annual shipments of roughly 100 to 120 tons of galena ore.
Additional carloads of ore were shipped after the main company operations had stopped.
Colorado's annual mining report listed the Quail Mine at Montezuma as a lead-silver operation.

moreHistory: USGS Professional Paper 178 describes two adits, each extending roughly 400 feet along the vein, with a raise connecting the lower and upper workings.
The surviving mine landscape includes openings, waste rock, rails, machinery, and collapsed timber remains associated with the historic operation.

sites.name: Reiling Dredge
overview: The Reiling Gold Dredge is a surviving early-twentieth-century placer-mining dredge in French Gulch east of Breckenridge. Built in 1908 for the French Gulch Dredging Company, it used a floating bucket-and-processing system to work gold-bearing gravel on an industrial scale.

Operations began in 1909 and the dredge worked the French Gulch landscape into the early 1920s. It partially sank in its pond in November 1922 and remained there, preserving a rare combination of dredge remains, pond, tailings, and associated mining landscape.

timeline.text: The Reiling Gold Dredge was constructed for the French Gulch Dredging Company.
Dredging operations began in the spring; early cleanups demonstrated the productivity of the French Gulch ground.
After later efforts to return the dredge to operation, it partially sank in November and was abandoned in the pond where it remains.
Colorado Preservation listed the Reiling Gold Dredge as one of Colorado's Most Endangered Places.
A preservation partnership stabilized portions of the deck and superstructure.
Colorado Preservation recognized the Reiling Gold Dredge as a saved historic resource after successful stabilization work.

moreHistory: Large gold dredges used bucket lines to excavate gravel, screens and sluices to recover gold, and conveyors to discard oversized rock. The resulting tailing piles remain a defining feature of French Gulch.

Preservation work has focused on retaining the dredge in place rather than reconstructing it as a new structure, allowing the surviving machinery and surrounding mining landscape to remain part of the interpretation.

sites.name: American Metals Incline
sites.componentDetail: Named historic mine incline shown on Copper Mountain topographic mapping
overview: American Metals Incline is a named historic mine feature in Summit County in the high country near Jacque Peak and Copper Mountain. U.S. Geological Survey-derived topographic mapping places the mine locality at approximately 39.44832, -106.19530.
Remnant uses the mapped mine locality as an identification point. The record does not claim that a mine opening is currently accessible, open, or safe.
